lede: The 10-year closes at its highest since 2007; futures steady; RBA hikes.
geo_headlines: THE 10-YEAR CLOSED AT 5.24%, ITS HIGHEST CLOSE SINCE JUNE 2007. Treasury's daily curve: the 10-year rose 7bp to 5.24%, the 2-year 11bp to 4.92% and the 30-year 7bp to 5.56%. The 10-year briefly touched 5.274% intraday (CNBC). **Real yields did all the work: the 10-year TIPS yield rose 7bp to 2.90%, so inflation expectations were flat.** The 2s10s curve flattened to 32bp as the front end repriced harder.

STOCKS FELL ON YIELDS, NOT ON FEAR. The S&P 500 fell 0.77% to 7,683.69 and the Dow lost 347 points; the Nasdaq 100 fell 1.08% and semis 1.61%. VIX rose to 16.07. The S&P is 1.48% below its August 13 record and the Nasdaq 100 1.48% below its September 22 record. After the bell, AMD agreed to buy World Labs for $8.2 billion and Nvidia authorized another $150 billion of buybacks earlier in the day (CNBC).

FEDWATCH NOW PUTS OCTOBER HIKE ODDS AT 70%. October 28 hike probability rose to 69.8% from 64.2% on Friday's data; a December hike is 94.8% priced, with 57.8% odds on a cumulative 50bp by then. Governor Cook said AI and oil are keeping inflation pressure up and further hikes are data dependent (investingLive). Barr speaks at 12:40 PM; his remarks helped drive last week's bond selloff.

AUSTRALIA HIKED TOO, TO A 15-YEAR HIGH. The RBA raised its cash rate 25bp to 4.60%, its fourth hike this year, citing energy costs (ABC). Westpac now expects another move in November. It is the same pattern as the Fed: oil-driven inflation is forcing central banks to keep tightening, even as growth slows.

IRAN IS WAITING ON A FORMAL US ANSWER; OIL IS FIRM BUT OFF ITS HIGHS. Araghchi met Qatari mediators and says Iran has not changed its seven-point plan; he expects Washington's formal reply via Qatar Tuesday (CBS). A US official called talks "positive and constructive" but says no deal without the nuclear file (Al Jazeera); Trump denied offering sanctions relief. November Brent was $106.77 (+1.4%) in Asia (Reuters); WTI has since faded to $91.72 (-0.95%).

FUTURES FLAT, ASIA MIXED, EUROPE HIGHER. S&P futures +0.08%, Nasdaq futures +0.24%. Japan's Topix fell 1.7% and the Nikkei 0.6%, led by refiners and power stocks; Australia and China edged up. The Stoxx 600 opened up about 0.4% despite higher oil. Gold +0.4% after Monday's 3% drop; bitcoin about $84,030.

JEFFERIES BEAT ON DEALS; TODAY BRINGS JOLTS AND CONFIDENCE. Jefferies earned $1.08 a share versus $1.00 expected, with investment banking up 17% and record equities trading; asset management fees fell (Reuters). JOLTS and Conference Board confidence are at 10:00 AM, Barr at 12:40 PM, Waller at 3:00 PM. Wednesday brings PCE; Friday's payrolls are expected around 85,000.
client_frame_short: The story this morning is interest rates, not headlines. The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.24% yesterday, its highest close since 2007, and stocks slipped less than 1%. **The whole rise was in real yields, meaning investors are demanding more return for lending, not bracing for more inflation.** Futures are flat this morning, and oil is firm but off its overnight highs. Nothing here calls for action; this is the best yield on safe money in nearly two decades, and Wednesday's inflation report and Friday's jobs report matter more than today.
client_frame:
If a client calls this morning, the headline they will have seen is that bond yields are at their highest since 2007. That is true, and it is the single most useful thing to explain today.

The 10-year Treasury closed at 5.24% on Monday, its highest close since June 2007. The 2-year rose even more, to 4.92%, because the market now sees about a 70% chance the Fed raises rates again on October 28 and almost certainly by December. Central banks are moving together: Australia raised rates overnight to a 15-year high, also citing energy costs.

The part worth slowing down on is why yields rose. Inflation-protected Treasury yields rose by the same amount, so the market's inflation expectation did not change. Investors are simply demanding a higher real return to lend money. That is a tighter financial environment, but it is not a panic signal, and it is not the market saying inflation is running away. It also matters for the mortgage and borrowing conversations clients are having: longer-term borrowing costs are set by these yields, so rates on new loans are likely to stay elevated until the Fed signals it is done.

Stocks are handling it in stride. The S&P 500 fell 0.77% Monday and is 1.48% below its August 13 record; futures are flat this morning. Oil is firm on the Iran standoff, with Iran awaiting a formal US answer through Qatar today, but it has not driven a new leg down in stocks.

For clients, the practical point is that cash and high-quality bonds are paying their best real returns in almost two decades. That is an opportunity for idle money and for anyone who needs income, not a reason to sell equities built for the long run. Locking in some of today's yields for several years is a reasonable conversation for clients with near-term spending needs. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.25% (we closed at 5.24%), a hot August PCE report on Wednesday, or Brent holding above $110.
